That is why the total momentum is conserved: Newton's third law is the reason behind the rule you use in the momentum section.

parts.title: Sorting the forces out
parts.question: A 2 kg bag sits on a shelf. (a) Name the two forces acting on the bag and explain why they are equal. (b) State the third-law partner of each.
steps: (a) Weight, $W = 2 \times 10 = 20$ N, acting downwards on the bag (the Earth's gravitational pull). The shelf's contact force, 20 N, acting upwards on the bag.
They are equal because the bag is at rest, so the resultant force on it must be zero — Newton's first law, not the third.
(b) Partner of the weight: the bag pulls the Earth upwards with a gravitational force of 20 N (acts on the Earth).
Partner of the shelf's push: the bag pushes the shelf downwards with a contact force of 20 N (acts on the shelf).
Each partner is the same type of force, the same size, opposite in direction, and acts on the other object.

questions.text: A cup rests on a desk. Its weight is 3 N and the desk pushes up on it with 3 N. Are these two forces a Newton's third law pair?
options: Yes — they are equal and opposite
No — they both act on the cup, and they are different types of force
Yes — they are the same size
No — third-law pairs are never equal
questions.explain: Equal and opposite is not enough. A third-law pair acts on two different objects and is the same type of force. These are balanced forces on one object (Newton's first law).

questions.text: A student says: "The weight of a book and the table pushing up on it are a Newton's third law pair because they are equal and opposite." Explain why the student is wrong.
questions.model:
• Both forces act on the same object (the book); third-law pair forces act on different objects.
  • They are different types of force (gravitational and contact); a third-law pair is always the same type.
  • They are equal because the book is in equilibrium (Newton's first law) — if the table were accelerating upwards in a lift, the push would be bigger than the weight, but a third-law pair is always equal.

questions.text: A cannon fires a cannonball. Which statement is correct?
options: The cannon exerts a bigger force on the ball than the ball exerts on the cannon, because the ball moves faster
The forces are equal; the ball accelerates more because its mass is much smaller
Only the ball experiences a force
The cannon exerts no force because it is heavy
questions.explain: Third-law forces are always equal. The ball's acceleration is large because a = F/m with a small m; the cannon's recoil acceleration is small for the same F and a large m.

questions.text: Use Newton's third law to explain why momentum is conserved when two trolleys collide.
questions.model:
• During the collision trolley A exerts a force on trolley B, and B exerts an equal and opposite force on A (Newton's third law).
  • The two forces act for the same time (the time they are in contact).
  • Force × time is the change in momentum, so A and B receive equal and opposite changes in momentum.
  • Whatever momentum one gains, the other loses, so the total momentum is unchanged.

questions.text: A car accelerates forwards. Its tyres push backwards on the road. Which force makes the car accelerate?
options: The road pushing forwards on the tyres
questions.explain: The tyres push the road backwards; by Newton's third law the road pushes the tyres (and so the car) forwards. The engine turns the wheels, but the forward force on the car comes from the road.

questions.text: A drone hovers at a constant height. Which pair of forces is a Newton's third law pair?
options: The drone's weight and the upward force from the air
The drone pushing air downwards and the air pushing the drone upwards
The drone's weight and the drone's thrust
The air pushing the drone up and the Earth pulling the drone down
questions.explain: Drone-on-air and air-on-drone: same type, equal, opposite, on different objects. Weight and the air's lift both act on the drone — they balance, but they are not a pair.

questions.text: A tennis racket hits a ball. Explain the forces involved in terms of Newton's third law. (2)
questions.model:
• The racket exerts a force on the ball, and the ball exerts a force on the racket — name both forces.
  • The two forces are equal in size and opposite in direction (and both are contact forces, acting on different objects).
questions.hint: Quoting the law scores one mark at most. Say what the two forces are in this collision — "the force of the racket on the ball" and "the force of the ball on the racket".

sections.title: Circular motion
sections.blurb: Constant speed, changing velocity, a resultant force towards the centre — and the word "centripetal" is a job description, not a new force.
checklist: Explain why an object moving in a circle at constant speed has a changing velocity
State that a resultant (centripetal) force acts towards the centre of the circle
Say which real force provides the centripetal force in a given situation
Predict what happens when the centripetal force is removed

parts.title: Constant speed but changing velocity
parts.html:
A satellite orbiting at a steady 7500 m/s, a car going round a roundabout at 10 m/s, a hammer being swung round a thrower's head: each has a constant speed. But velocity is a vector, and the direction is changing all the time — so the velocity is changing.

A changing velocity is an acceleration. By Newton's first law, an accelerating object must have a resultant force on it. For circular motion that resultant force acts towards the centre of the circle — at right angles to the velocity, which is why it changes the direction and not the speed. We call it the centripetal force ("centre-seeking").

Centripetal force is not an extra force. It is the name for whichever real force happens to be doing the job of pulling the object towards the centre:

SituationWhat provides the centripetal force
Satellite or planet in orbitGravity
Car going round a bend or roundaboutFriction between the tyres and the road
Ball on a string, hammer throwTension in the string / wire
Clothes in a spinning washing machine drumThe contact (normal) force from the drum
Electron orbiting a nucleus (old model)Electrostatic attraction

Remove the force (the string breaks, the road is icy) and the object no longer accelerates: it carries on in a straight line at a tangent to the circle, at the speed it had — Newton's first law again.

parts.title: A satellite in orbit
parts.question: A satellite moves in a circular orbit around the Earth at a constant speed. Explain why it is accelerating, and state what provides the force.
steps: Velocity is a vector: speed and direction.
The satellite's speed is constant, but its direction of motion is continually changing as it goes round the circle.
So its velocity is changing, and a changing velocity means it is accelerating.
An acceleration needs a resultant force. Here it is the Earth's gravitational pull on the satellite, which acts towards the centre of the Earth — the centre of the orbit.
Gravity is the centripetal force. It acts at right angles to the velocity, so it changes the direction of motion without changing the speed.

questions.text: A car drives round a roundabout at a steady 8 m/s. Explain why the car's velocity is changing even though its speed is not.
questions.model:
• Velocity is a vector quantity — it has a direction as well as a size.
  • The car's direction of motion is continually changing as it goes round the roundabout.
  • So its velocity is changing (and it is accelerating) even though its speed stays at 8 m/s.

questions.text: Which force provides the centripetal force on a car going round a roundabout?
options: Friction between the tyres and the road
questions.explain: Friction from the road acts sideways on the tyres, towards the centre of the roundabout. On ice there is little friction, which is why cars slide straight on.

questions.text: In which direction does the resultant force act on an object moving in a circle at constant speed?
options: Opposite to the direction of motion
Towards the centre of the circle
Away from the centre of the circle
questions.explain: Towards the centre. If it had a component along the motion the speed would change; a force at right angles only changes the direction.

questions.text: A hammer thrower swings the hammer in a circle on a wire. What provides the centripetal force?
questions.explain: The wire pulls the hammer inwards towards the thrower: tension. Momentum is not a force.

questions.text: A ball is whirled round on a string. Describe and explain what happens to the ball if the string snaps.
questions.model:
• The ball moves off in a straight line, along a tangent to the circle (not outwards along the radius).
  • It keeps the speed it had at that moment.
  • Because the tension — the centripetal force — has gone, there is no resultant force, so by Newton's first law the ball continues at constant velocity.

questions.text: Which statement about centripetal force is correct?
options: It is an extra force that appears whenever something moves in a circle
It is the name given to whichever force acts towards the centre, such as gravity or tension
It acts outwards, which is why you feel pushed to the outside on a roundabout
It is only present for objects moving at high speed
questions.explain: Centripetal is a role, not a new force. The outward feeling on a roundabout is your body trying to go straight on (Newton's first law) while the car turns under you.

sections.title: Inertial mass
sections.blurb: Mass as a measure of how hard it is to change an object's velocity — defined as force ÷ acceleration — and why it is not the same idea as weight.
checklist: Explain what inertial mass measures
State that inertial mass is defined as the ratio of force to acceleration
Explain why inertial mass does not change on the Moon even though weight does

parts.title: Mass as resistance to changing velocity
parts.html:
Inertia is the tendency of an object to keep doing what it is doing — to stay at rest, or to keep moving at constant velocity (Newton's first law).

Inertial mass is a measure of how difficult it is to change the velocity of an object — to get it moving from rest, to speed it up, slow it down, or change its direction. It is defined as the ratio of force to acceleration:

$$\text{inertial mass} = \dfrac{F}{a}$$

So if the same force gives one object half the acceleration of another, the first object has twice the inertial mass. This is just $F = ma$ rearranged, but the exam wants the idea: mass is what makes velocity hard to change.

Inertial massWeight
MeasuresResistance to accelerationThe pull of gravity
Found from$F \div a$$m \times g$
On the MoonUnchanged — a 1000 kg buggy is just as hard to push into motionAbout one sixth
In deep space (no gravity)UnchangedZero

An astronaut floating in orbit is "weightless", but a loaded cargo pallet is still hard to push: its inertial mass is the same as on Earth.

parts.title: Comparing inertial masses
parts.question: A resultant force of 12 N gives trolley A an acceleration of 3 m/s². The same force gives trolley B an acceleration of 1.5 m/s². Calculate the inertial mass of each trolley and say which is harder to get moving.
steps: Trolley B has twice the inertial mass: for the same force it accelerates half as much, so it is harder to change its velocity.

questions.text: A resultant force of 50 N gives a crate an acceleration of 2.5 m/s². Calculate the inertial mass of the crate.
questions.hint: Force divided by acceleration.

questions.text: A 20 N push gives a loaded trolley an acceleration of 8 m/s². Calculate its inertial mass.
questions.hint: m = F ÷ a.

questions.text: Explain what is meant by the inertial mass of an object.
questions.model:
• A measure of how difficult it is to change the velocity of the object (including starting it from rest).
  • It is defined as the ratio of the force applied to the acceleration produced: m = F ÷ a.

questions.text: The same resultant force is applied to a tennis ball and to a bowling ball. Which statement is correct?
options: The bowling ball accelerates less because it has more inertial mass
The bowling ball accelerates more because it is heavier
The tennis ball accelerates less because it is lighter
questions.explain: a = F ÷ m: with the same F, the larger mass gets the smaller acceleration. The bowling ball's velocity is harder to change.

questions.text: On Earth a shopping trolley needs a resultant force of 50 N to accelerate at 2 m/s². On the Moon, what resultant force would give the same trolley the same acceleration?
questions.hint: Inertial mass does not depend on gravity.
walkthrough: Inertial mass $= \dfrac{50}{2} = 25$ kg — the same on the Moon.
$F = m \times a = 25 \times 2 = 50$ N, exactly as on Earth.
Its weight on the Moon is smaller (about 40 N instead of 250 N), but its resistance to acceleration is unchanged.

questions.text: An astronaut in orbit is "weightless". Which statement about a 500 kg satellite she is trying to push is correct?
options: It is easy to push because it has no weight
It is just as hard to accelerate as on Earth because its inertial mass is unchanged
It cannot be moved at all
It has no mass in orbit
questions.explain: Weight depends on gravity; inertial mass does not. Changing the satellite's velocity needs the same force in orbit as it would on Earth.

sections.title: Conservation of momentum
sections.blurb: Total momentum before = total momentum after, as long as no outside force acts. The method is always the same; the directions are where it goes wrong.
checklist: Apply conservation of momentum to objects that stick together
Use a sign convention so that opposite directions have opposite signs
Handle explosions and recoil, where the total momentum is zero
Find the velocity of one object after a collision when the other's is known
Explain, using Newton's third law, why momentum is conserved in a collision or explosion (four steps)

parts.title: Before equals after
parts.html:
In any collision or explosion where no external force acts (a closed system), the total momentum is conserved: the total before equals the total after. This follows from Newton's third law (see the pairs section).

$$\text{total momentum before} = \text{total momentum after}$$

Method, every time:

  1. Choose a positive direction (usually the direction the first object moves). Anything moving the other way gets a minus sign.
  2. Write the momentum of each object before: $m \times v$ each, with signs. Add them.
  3. Write the momentum of each object after, using a symbol for the unknown velocity. Add them.
  4. Set before = after and solve. A negative answer means that object moves in the negative direction.
TypeWhat to watch
Objects stick togetherAfter the collision there is one object with the combined mass and one velocity
Head-on collisionThe two velocities before have opposite signs
Explosion / recoil (gun, rocket, skater throwing something)Total momentum before is zero, so afterwards the two momenta are equal and opposite
One object's final velocity givenPut it in; the other final velocity is the unknown

parts.title: Sticking together
parts.question: A 2 kg trolley moving at 3 m/s collides with a stationary 1 kg trolley. They stick together. Calculate their velocity after the collision.
steps: Positive direction: the direction of the moving trolley.
After: one object of mass $2 + 1 = 3$ kg at velocity $v$: $p = 3v$.
Conservation: $3v = 6$, so $v = 2$ m/s, in the original direction of the 2 kg trolley.

parts.title: Why momentum is conserved: Newton's third law
parts.html:
Conservation of momentum is not a separate rule to memorise — it follows from Newton's third law. The chain of reasoning the exam wants, in order:

  1. When the two bodies collide, each exerts a force on the other. By Newton's third law the forces are the same size on each body and in opposite directions.
  2. The two forces act for the same time — the time the bodies are in contact.
  3. Force × time is the change in momentum ($F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{t}$, so $\Delta p = F \times t$). Equal forces for equal times give changes in momentum that are equal in size and opposite in direction.
  4. So the total change in momentum is zero: whatever momentum one body gains, the other loses. The total momentum after equals the total before.

Four steps, four marks. Leave out "for the same time" and the argument does not work — equal forces for different times would give different changes in momentum.

parts.title: The explanation as an exam answer
parts.question: Two trolleys collide on a frictionless track. Explain, using Newton's third law, why the total momentum of the trolleys is the same after the collision as before. (4)
steps: 1. During the collision trolley A exerts a force on trolley B, and trolley B exerts a force on trolley A that is equal in size and opposite in direction (Newton's third law).
2. The two forces act for the same time, because the trolleys are in contact for the same time.
3. Change in momentum = force × time, so the trolleys receive changes in momentum that are equal in size and opposite in direction.
4. The changes cancel: the total change in momentum is zero, so the total momentum is unchanged by the collision.
Each numbered line is one mark. The same answer, with \"the ball and the bat\" or \"the gun and the bullet\" substituted, answers every version of the question.

questions.text: A 1500 kg car travelling at 10 m/s runs into the back of a stationary 1000 kg car. The two cars lock together. Calculate their velocity immediately after the collision.
questions.hint: Momentum before is all in the moving car. After, the combined mass is 2500 kg.

questions.text: A 4 kg rifle fires a 20 g bullet at 300 m/s. Calculate the recoil speed of the rifle (just the size).
questions.hint: Before firing the total momentum is zero, so afterwards the rifle's momentum is equal and opposite to the bullet's. 20 g = 0.02 kg.
walkthrough: $6 + 4v = 0$, so $v = -1.5$ m/s. The rifle recoils at 1.5 m/s in the opposite direction to the bullet.

questions.text: A 2 kg trolley moving to the right at 4 m/s collides head-on with a 3 kg trolley moving to the left at 1 m/s. They stick together. Calculate their velocity after the collision (take right as positive).
questions.hint: The 3 kg trolley's velocity is −1 m/s.

questions.text: A 0.5 kg snooker ball moving at 6 m/s hits an identical stationary ball. After the collision the first ball continues in the same direction at 2 m/s. Calculate the velocity of the second ball.
questions.hint: The balls do not stick. Put in the first ball's final velocity; the second ball's is the unknown.
walkthrough: $1 + 0.5v = 3$, so $v = 4$ m/s in the original direction.

questions.text: State what is meant by "momentum is conserved" in a collision, and give the condition for it to be true.
questions.model:
• The total momentum of the objects before the collision equals the total momentum after it.
  • This is true provided no external (outside) forces act on the system — it is a closed system.

questions.text: A 50 kg skater standing still on ice throws a 5 kg bag horizontally at 4 m/s. Calculate the skater's recoil speed (just the size).
questions.hint: Total momentum before is zero.
walkthrough: $20 + 50v = 0$, so $v = -0.4$ m/s: the skater moves at 0.4 m/s the opposite way to the bag.

questions.text: A cannon fires a cannonball. Explain, using Newton's third law, why the cannon recoils with the same size of momentum as the cannonball. (4)
questions.model:
• The cannon exerts a force on the ball and the ball exerts a force on the cannon that is equal in size and opposite in direction (Newton's third law).
  • The two forces act for the same time (while the ball is being pushed along the barrel).
  • Change in momentum = force × time, so the ball and the cannon gain changes in momentum that are equal in size and opposite in direction.
  • The total momentum was zero before firing, so it is zero after: the cannon's momentum backwards equals the ball's momentum forwards.

questions.text: In the Newton's-third-law explanation of momentum conservation, why does it matter that the two forces act for the same time?
options: Because change in momentum = force × time, so equal forces for equal times give equal and opposite changes in momentum
Because the forces are only equal while the objects are moving
Because momentum is measured in seconds
questions.explain: Equal forces alone are not enough: the change in momentum each body receives is F × t, so the times must be equal too for the changes to cancel.

sections.title: Force = change in momentum ÷ time, and safety features
sections.blurb: Why airbags, crumple zones, seatbelts and helmets work: the momentum change is fixed, so make the time longer and the force gets smaller.
checklist: Use F = (mv − mu) ÷ t to find a force, a time or a change in momentum
Explain how a safety feature reduces injury, using momentum, time and force in the right order
Explain why large decelerations are dangerous

parts.title: Newton's second law, momentum version
parts.html:
$$\text{force} = \dfrac{\text{change in momentum}}{\text{time}}\qquad F = \dfrac{mv - mu}{t}$$

The change in momentum is $mv - mu$: final momentum minus initial momentum. For something stopping, $v = 0$, so the change is just $-mu$ (the size of the force is $mu \div t$; the minus sign says it acts against the motion).

The key idea: in a collision the change in momentum is fixed — the car is going to stop. The only thing a safety feature can change is how long the stopping takes. A longer time means a smaller force, and it is the force that does the damage.

FeatureHow it increases the time
Crumple zoneThe front of the car crushes progressively instead of stopping dead
AirbagCushions the head: it stops over the depth of the bag, not against the hard dashboard
SeatbeltStretches slightly, and stops the person over the same time as the car rather than when they hit the windscreen
Cycle helmetFoam compresses on impact
Crash mat, bending your knees on landingSame idea: longer stopping time

The 4-mark answer, in order: (1) the momentum change is the same with or without the feature; (2) the feature increases the time taken to stop; (3) force = change in momentum ÷ time, so (4) the force on the person is smaller, so less injury. Students who write "it absorbs the impact" get nothing.

Large decelerations are dangerous because a large deceleration means a large force on the body ($F = ma$). Forces of many times a person's weight can break bones, tear organs and injure the brain against the skull — even without hitting anything, because the body's own tissues have to supply the stopping force.

parts.title: With and without an airbag
parts.question: A 60 kg driver is travelling at 15 m/s when the car crashes and stops. (a) Calculate the force on the driver if she stops in 0.05 s against the steering wheel. (b) Calculate the force if an airbag increases her stopping time to 0.3 s.
steps: Change in momentum $= mv - mu = (60 \times 0) - (60 \times 15) = -900$ kg m/s (the size is 900 kg m/s, acting against her motion).
Same change in momentum, six times the time, one sixth of the force.

questions.text: A 0.16 kg cricket ball travelling at 30 m/s is caught and brought to rest in 0.02 s. Calculate the size of the average force on the ball.
questions.hint: Change in momentum is 0.16 × 30, then divide by the time.
walkthrough: Change in momentum $= (0.16 \times 0) - (0.16 \times 30) = -4.8$ kg m/s: a size of 4.8 kg m/s, against the ball's motion.

questions.text: A 1200 kg car travelling at 20 m/s hits a wall and stops in 0.5 s. Calculate the size of the average force on the car.
walkthrough: Change in momentum $= 0 - (1200 \times 20) = -24\,000$ kg m/s: a size of 24 000 kg m/s.
Units: N (48 kN, acting against the motion)

questions.text: A 70 kg passenger without a seatbelt is moving at 12 m/s when the car stops suddenly. He hits the dashboard and stops in 0.1 s. Calculate the size of the force on him.
questions.hint: Momentum change 70 × 12, time 0.1 s.
walkthrough: Change in momentum $= 0 - (70 \times 12) = -840$ kg m/s: a size of 840 kg m/s.

questions.text: A 60 kg gymnast lands from a vault at 10 m/s. The maximum safe force on her legs is 2000 N. Calculate the minimum time she must take to stop.
questions.hint: Rearrange: t = change in momentum ÷ force.
walkthrough: She bends her knees so that the stop takes at least 0.3 s.

questions.text: Explain how an airbag reduces the injury to a driver in a crash.
questions.model:
• The driver's change in momentum is the same whether or not the airbag is there (she goes from her speed to rest).
  • The airbag increases the time taken for her head to stop.
  • Force = change in momentum ÷ time, so a longer time means a smaller force on her.
  • A smaller force means less injury.

questions.text: Which of these is the reason a crumple zone reduces the force on passengers?
options: It reduces the change in momentum of the car
It increases the time over which the car's momentum changes
It increases the mass of the car
It makes the car stop more quickly
questions.explain: The momentum change is fixed by the car's speed. A crumple zone makes the stop take longer, and F = Δp ÷ t gets smaller.

questions.text: Explain why a large deceleration is dangerous for a person in a vehicle.
questions.model:
• A large deceleration means a large resultant force on the person (F = ma).
  • The force on the body can be many times the person's weight.
  • Such forces can break bones, damage internal organs, or injure the brain as it strikes the inside of the skull.

questions.text: A tennis ball of mass 0.16 kg travels towards a racket at 20 m/s. The racket hits it and it leaves in the opposite direction at 25 m/s. The ball is in contact with the racket for 70 ms.

parts.text: Calculate the change in momentum of the ball. (Give the size.)
parts.hint: Velocity is a vector. Take the direction towards the racket as positive: u = +20 m/s, v = −25 m/s. The change is v − u, not the difference of the two sizes.
walkthrough: Take towards the racket as positive: $u = +20$ m/s, $v = -25$ m/s.
Size of the change: 7.2 kg m/s (the minus sign says it is directed away from the racket). Subtracting $4 - 3.2 = 0.8$ ignores the change of direction and scores one mark at most.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Calculate the average force the racket exerts on the ball.
parts.hint: 70 ms is 0.070 s — ms means milliseconds.
walkthrough: Using 70 instead of 0.070 gives 0.1 N — a force smaller than the weight of a feather, which is the sense check that catches it.
parts.label: b

sections.title: Braking distance and speed squared
sections.blurb: The brakes do work to remove the car's kinetic energy. Because KE depends on v², doubling the speed quadruples the braking distance.
checklist: Use work done = kinetic energy to calculate a braking distance or a braking force
Explain why braking distance is proportional to speed squared
Estimate how stopping distance changes across typical speeds (thinking ∝ v, braking ∝ v²)

parts.title: Work done by the brakes = kinetic energy lost
parts.html:
To stop a car, the brakes must remove all of its kinetic energy. The braking force does work over the braking distance:

$$\text{work done} = F \times d\qquad\qquad KE = \tfrac{1}{2} \times m \times v^2$$

Setting them equal:

$$\tfrac{1}{2} m v^2 = F \times d\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad d = \dfrac{\tfrac{1}{2} m v^2}{F}$$

The braking force $F$ is roughly constant for a given car and road (it depends on the brakes, tyres and surface). So:

  • Braking distance ∝ $v^2$. Double the speed → four times the braking distance. Treble it → nine times.
  • Thinking distance ∝ $v$, because it is speed × reaction time. Double the speed → double the thinking distance.
  • A heavier car (more $m$) or a wet road (less $F$) also increases the braking distance.
SpeedThinking distanceBraking distanceStopping distance
20 mph (9 m/s)6 m6 m12 m
30 mph (13 m/s)9 m14 m23 m
40 mph (18 m/s)12 m24 m36 m
50 mph (22 m/s)15 m38 m53 m
60 mph (27 m/s)18 m55 m73 m
70 mph (31 m/s)21 m75 m96 m

(Highway Code figures, for a dry road and an alert driver.) Notice the thinking column goes up in equal steps; the braking column grows faster and faster.

parts.title: Braking distance from work done
parts.question: A 1200 kg car travelling at 20 m/s brakes with a constant braking force of 6000 N. Calculate its braking distance.
steps: The brakes do this much work: $F \times d = 240\,000$.

questions.text: The same 1200 kg car with the same 6000 N braking force is now travelling at 30 m/s. Calculate its braking distance.
questions.hint: KE = ½ × 1200 × 30². Then divide by 6000 N.
walkthrough: 1.5 times the speed gives $1.5^2 = 2.25$ times the braking distance ($2.25 \times 40 = 90$ m). ✓

questions.text: A 1000 kg car travelling at 15 m/s stops in a braking distance of 25 m. Calculate the average braking force.
questions.hint: Find the KE, then F = KE ÷ d.

questions.text: A driver doubles her speed. What happens to the braking distance?
questions.explain: Braking distance ∝ v². Doubling v multiplies v² by 4, so the braking distance is four times as long. (Thinking distance only doubles.)

questions.text: At 30 mph (13 m/s) a car's thinking distance is 9 m and its braking distance is 14 m. Estimate its stopping distance at 60 mph (26 m/s).
questions.hint: Thinking distance doubles; braking distance goes up by 2² = 4.
walkthrough: Stopping distance $\approx 18 + 56 = 74$ m — roughly three times the 23 m at 30 mph, not twice.

questions.text: Explain why the braking distance of a car is proportional to the square of its speed.
questions.model:
• The brakes must do work equal to the car's kinetic energy to stop it: F × d = ½mv².
  • The braking force F is roughly constant (it depends on the brakes, tyres and road, not on speed).
  • So d = ½mv² ÷ F, and d is proportional to v²: doubling the speed quadruples the braking distance.

questions.text: Which factor increases the braking distance by reducing the braking force?
options: A heavier load in the car
questions.explain: Water or ice reduces the friction between the tyres and the road, so the braking force is smaller and the same KE takes a longer distance to remove. A heavier load increases the KE instead.

sections.title: Core practical: the analysis
sections.blurb: Why the masses move from trolley to hanger, how two light gates give an acceleration, what friction does to the graph, and what the gradient means.
checklist: Calculate an acceleration from two light-gate readings and the time between them
Explain why the total mass must stay constant when investigating force
Explain how to compensate for friction, and how friction shows up on the graph
Interpret the gradient and intercept of an acceleration–force graph

parts.title: From light-gate times to an acceleration
parts.html:
With two light gates the data logger (or you) does three calculations:

  1. Speed at gate 1: $v_1 = \text{card length} \div \text{time through gate 1}$.
  2. Speed at gate 2: $v_2 = \text{card length} \div \text{time through gate 2}$.
  3. Acceleration: $a = (v_2 - v_1) \div \text{time to travel from gate 1 to gate 2}$.

Keep the units straight: card length in metres, times in seconds.

Why the masses move from the trolley to the hanger. The hanging weight accelerates the whole system — trolley plus hanging mass — because they are joined by the string. If you simply added more mass to the hanger you would increase the force and the mass at the same time, so you could not tell which caused the change in acceleration. Moving a mass from the trolley to the hanger changes only the force; the total mass is unchanged.

Friction. Friction on the trolley opposes the motion, so the resultant force is less than the hanging weight. Two ways to deal with it:

  • Compensate: tilt the runway slightly, until the trolley (given a gentle push, with no hanging mass) runs at a constant speed. The component of its weight down the slope now cancels friction.
  • Or leave it and read it off the graph: uncompensated friction gives an acceleration–force graph that is still a straight line, but it cuts the force axis at a positive value. That intercept is the friction force — the force you need before the trolley accelerates at all.

The gradient. From $F = ma$, $a = F \times \dfrac{1}{m}$, so the gradient of $a$ against $F$ is $\dfrac{1}{m}$: the reciprocal of the total mass. A plot of $a$ against $m$ (force constant) is a curve, because $a = F \div m$; to get a straight line, plot $a$ against $\dfrac{1}{m}$.

parts.title: Acceleration from two light gates
parts.question: A 10 cm card on a trolley takes 0.050 s to pass through the first light gate and 0.025 s to pass through the second. The trolley takes 0.4 s to travel between the gates. Calculate its acceleration.

questions.text: A trolley carries an 8 cm card. It takes 0.040 s to pass the first light gate and 0.020 s to pass the second, and 0.5 s to travel between the gates.

parts.text: Calculate the speed at the first gate.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Calculate the speed at the second gate.
parts.hint: Same card, shorter time.
parts.label: b

parts.text: Calculate the acceleration of the trolley.
parts.hint: Change in velocity between the gates ÷ time between the gates.
parts.label: c

questions.text: A student investigates how acceleration depends on force. Explain why she moves masses from the trolley onto the hanger, rather than adding new masses to the hanger.
questions.model:
• The hanging weight accelerates both the trolley and the hanging masses, because they are connected.
  • Adding new masses would increase the force and the total mass at the same time, so two variables would change.
  • Moving a mass from the trolley to the hanger increases the force but keeps the total accelerated mass constant — a fair test.

questions.text: Describe how to compensate for friction before starting the experiment.
questions.model:
• Remove the hanging mass and give the trolley a gentle push.
  • Raise the end of the runway (tilt it) a little at a time,
  • until the trolley moves along it at a constant speed (the light gates can check this).
  • The component of the trolley's weight down the slope now balances friction, so the hanging weight is the resultant force.

questions.text: The graph shows another student's results for acceleration against force, with the total mass kept constant. She did not compensate for friction.

parts.text: Calculate the gradient of the line.
parts.hint: Use the points X (0.5, 0) and Y (3, 5).
parts.label: a

parts.text: Use the gradient to find the total mass of the trolley and hanging masses.
parts.hint: Gradient = 1 ÷ mass.
parts.label: b

parts.text: What does the intercept on the force axis (0.5 N at X) tell you?
options: The friction force on the trolley
parts.explain: The trolley does not accelerate until the force exceeds 0.5 N — that is the friction that has to be overcome first. A compensated runway would move the line to pass through the origin.
parts.label: c

graph.alt: Acceleration against force: a straight line from (0.5, 0) to (3, 5), not through the origin.

questions.text: A student plots acceleration against mass with the force kept constant. What shape of graph should she expect?
options: A straight line through the origin
A curve, because a = F ÷ m
A straight line with a positive intercept
questions.explain: With F constant, a is inversely proportional to m — a curve that falls as m increases. Plotting a against 1/m gives a straight line through the origin.

sections.title: Apply the seven steps: the trolley practical
sections.blurb: The seven-step recipe for a "describe how you would investigate" question is in Topic 1. Here it is applied to this topic's core practical, with two 6-mark questions to write in full.
checklist: Write a full 6-mark method for the force–mass–acceleration practical using the seven steps
Say what is changed, what is measured and with what, and what is done with the results
Give one accuracy detail, and say you will repeat and calculate a mean

parts.title: The seven steps, in one line each
parts.html:
From Topic 1, T6: (1) the two variables; (2) the formula that links them; (3) what you change and how, and what you keep the same; (4) what you measure, how, and with what equipment; (5) what you do with the results — a calculation or a graph; (6) one detail that makes the results accurate; (7) repeat the readings and calculate a mean. One mark each; the question is out of six, so any six of the seven score.

For this practical the equipment is the trolley on a runway, a string over a pulley to a mass hanger, a card and two light gates with a data logger. The worked example below shows the recipe applied to force and acceleration; the questions use the same kit for mass, and for a ramp.

parts.title: Where the marks go missing
parts.html: The two most common ways to lose marks are describing the equipment without saying what you measure with it ("use light gates" earns nothing; "use light gates to record the speed at each point" does), and stopping after you have collected the data. The question asked how you would investigate the link between the two variables, so the calculation or graph that shows the link is a mark in its own right. And the easiest mark on the paper is the one most often thrown away: "repeat" alone scores nothing — "repeat and calculate a mean" scores.

parts.title: How the 6-mark question is marked
parts.html:
Edexcel marks the 6-mark "describe how you would investigate" question in levels, not point by point. For the force–mass–acceleration practical the mark scheme separates isolated statements from details of the procedure:

Isolated statements (naming things)Details of the procedure (saying what is done with them)
weights on hanger; weights added to trolley; light gates / ticker timer; data logger; card on trolley; sloping runway; weigh the trolley; use $a = (v - u) \div t$; plot a graph of $F$ against $a$suspend weights from the hanger to produce the force; change the force by changing the weights on the hanger; keep the mass constant by moving weights between hanger and trolley; light gates used to measure velocity / time; runway sloped so the trolley rolls at constant speed with no force (friction compensated); interrupter card for the time through the gate
LevelMarksNeeds
11–2at least two isolated statements ("add weights", "use light gates")
23–4one detail of procedure plus one other statement
35–6two details of procedure plus one other statement, in a clear, logical order

So the difference between 2 marks and 6 is saying what each piece of equipment is for. "Use light gates" is a statement; "use light gates to measure the velocity at two points" is a procedure. The seven steps produce procedure details automatically — steps 3, 4 and 6 are each one.

parts.title: Investigating force and acceleration
parts.question: Describe how you would investigate how the acceleration of a trolley depends on the resultant force acting on it. (6 marks)
steps: Step 1 — the two variables. I am investigating force (independent variable, the one I change) and acceleration (dependent variable, the one I measure).
Step 2 — the formula. They are linked by $F = m \times a$. That means the mass must be kept constant, and at the end I expect $a$ to be proportional to $F$.

Step 3 — what I change and how. The force is the weight of a mass hanging on a string that runs over a pulley to the trolley. I change the force by moving a slotted mass from the trolley to the hanger, so that the total mass being accelerated stays the same. I use five different forces.

Step 4 — what I measure and how. I put a card of known length on the trolley and set up two light gates connected to a data logger. The data logger records the speed at each gate and the time to travel between them. I measure the distance between the gates with a metre rule.

Step 5 — what I do with the results. I calculate the acceleration with $a = (v - u) \div t$ from the two speeds and the time between the gates, then plot a graph of $a$ against $F$. A straight line through the origin shows that $a \propto F$; the gradient is $1 \div m$.

Step 6 — accuracy. I release the trolley from the same marked point each time, and I tilt the runway slightly first so that the trolley runs at a constant speed with no hanging mass — this compensates for friction, so the hanging weight is the only resultant force.
Step 7 — repeat and mean. I repeat the readings for each force three times and calculate a mean acceleration for each force before plotting.

As it would be written in the exam: seven numbered sentences, one per step — about ten lines. Every sentence contains either a variable, a piece of equipment and what it measures, or what is done with a number.

parts.title: Planning a practical
parts.intro: Write the full answer on paper, as seven numbered points, before you open the mark scheme. Then mark yourself one mark per row — the question is out of six, so any six of the seven rows score.

questions.text: A student has a trolley, a set of slotted masses, a mass hanger, a string and pulley, a card, two light gates and a data logger. Describe how the student could investigate how the acceleration of the trolley depends on its mass. (6 marks)
questions.model:
6 marks — one mark per row below, any six of the seven.

PointForWhat you need to write
1VariablesIdentifies the two variables: the mass of the trolley is changed (independent) and the acceleration is measured (dependent).
2FormulaStates that they are linked by $F = m \times a$ (or $a = F \div m$).
3ChangeChanges the mass by adding slotted masses to the trolley, using at least five different masses, and keeps the force the same by leaving the same mass on the hanger every time.
4MeasureMeasures the acceleration using the card and two light gates with a data logger: speed at each gate, time between the gates, $a = (v - u) \div t$ (or the data logger calculates it).
5Use the resultPlots a graph of acceleration against mass (or against $1 \div \text{mass}$) and describes the link — $a$ decreases as $m$ increases; $a$ against $1/m$ is a straight line through the origin with gradient $F$.
6AccuracyOne specific detail that makes the results accurate: releases the trolley from the same marked point each time, or tilts the runway to compensate for friction, or measures the card length precisely with a ruler.
7Repeat & meanRepeats the readings for each mass and calculates a mean. "Repeat" on its own does not score.
  • "Use light gates" on its own does not earn the Measure mark — you must say what the light gates measure.
  • The Use the result mark needs a graph or a calculation that links the two variables, not just "record the results in a table".
questions.hint: Step 1: the variables are mass and acceleration. Which one will you add masses to change, and what must then stay the same?

questions.text: A trolley is released from rest at the top of a ramp. Describe how you would investigate how the velocity of the trolley depends on the distance it has travelled down the ramp. (6 marks)
questions.model:
6 marks — one mark per row below, any six of the seven.

PointForWhat you need to write
1VariablesIdentifies the two variables: the distance travelled down the ramp is changed (independent) and the velocity at that point is measured (dependent).
2FormulaStates that they are linked by $v^2 - u^2 = 2 \times a \times x$, and that $u = 0$ because the trolley starts from rest (so $v^2 = 2ax$).
3ChangeChanges the distance by moving a light gate to different positions down the ramp, measuring the distance from the release point to the gate with a metre rule, for at least five distances.
4MeasureMeasures the velocity at the gate: a card of measured length on the trolley breaks the light-gate beam, the timer records the time, and velocity $= \text{card length} \div \text{time}$.
5Use the resultPlots a graph of $v^2$ against $x$. A straight line through the origin shows that $v^2 \propto x$ (the acceleration is constant); the gradient equals $2a$, so the acceleration is half the gradient.
6AccuracyOne specific detail that makes the results accurate: releases the trolley from the same marked point each time without pushing it, or keeps the ramp at the same angle throughout, or measures the distance to the gate from the front of the card.
7Repeat & meanRepeats the readings at each distance and calculates a mean velocity. "Repeat" on its own does not score.
  • Plotting $v$ against $x$ and saying "it curves" earns the graph part of the last mark only if you say the curve shows $v$ is not proportional to $x$; the full mark needs $v^2$ against $x$.
  • A stopwatch instead of a light gate is accepted for the Measure mark only if you say what distance and time you would use to find the velocity, and note that reaction time makes it less accurate.
questions.hint: Which equation has velocity, distance and no time in it? What does it say you should plot to get a straight line?

sections.title: Measuring reaction time
sections.blurb: The ruler-drop test and the computer test: how each works, the maths that turns a drop distance into a time, and why neither is quite the same as reacting while driving.
checklist: Describe the ruler-drop and computer-click methods of measuring reaction time
Convert a ruler-drop distance into a reaction time using x = ½gt²
Evaluate the methods: repeats, anticipation, and the difference from a real driving situation

parts.title: Two methods
parts.html:
Ruler dropComputer test
A partner holds a ruler vertically with the zero level with your open thumb and finger. Without warning they let go; you catch it as quickly as you can. Read the distance it fell. Repeat several times and take a mean.A program shows a signal (a colour change, a sound) at a random moment; you click or press a key as fast as you can. The computer records the time directly, in milliseconds. Repeat and take a mean.
Gives a distance; you convert it to a time.Gives the time directly, more precisely.

Converting the drop distance. The ruler falls freely from rest, so with $u = 0$ and $a = g$:

$$x = \tfrac{1}{2} g t^2\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2x}{g}}$$

Use the distance in metres. A 20 cm drop gives $t = \sqrt{2 \times 0.2 \div 10} = 0.2$ s. (Edexcel do not require you to derive this; they do expect you to use it.)

Evaluating. Repeating and averaging reduces random error. Problems: the catcher may anticipate the drop (so the partner must vary the timing); the catching reaction uses the hand, whereas a driver's foot has further to move to the brake, so real braking reaction times are longer; and a test done when alert does not show the effect of tiredness, alcohol or distraction. Typical results: 0.2–0.3 s for a hand catch; 0.5–0.9 s for a driver.

parts.title: Reaction time from a ruler drop
parts.question: A student catches a dropped ruler after it has fallen 20 cm. Calculate her reaction time. (g = 10 m/s².)

questions.text: A ruler falls 45 cm before it is caught. Calculate the reaction time.
A student's reaction time is 0.25 s. How far, in cm, will a ruler fall before she catches it?
questions.hint: x = ½gt², then convert metres to centimetres.

questions.text: Explain why the ruler-drop test should be repeated several times and a mean taken.
questions.model:
• Reaction time varies from one attempt to the next (random variation).
  • Repeating and averaging reduces the effect of this random error and makes the result more reliable.
  • Any anomalous result (e.g. an anticipated catch) can be spotted and left out.

questions.text: Which is an advantage of the computer test over the ruler drop?
options: It measures the time directly and more precisely
It uses a longer reaction time
It measures the driver's braking time exactly
questions.explain: The computer times the response in milliseconds with no conversion needed. It still needs repeats, and it is still a hand response, not a foot-on-brake response.

questions.text: In a ruler-drop test, student A catches the ruler at 15 cm and student B at 30 cm. Which statement is correct?
options: A has the slower reaction time
B has the slower reaction time
They have the same reaction time
B's reaction time is exactly twice A's
questions.explain: A longer drop means the ruler fell for longer before it was caught — a slower reaction. Because x ∝ t², doubling the distance makes the time √2 ≈ 1.4 times longer, not twice.

questions.text: Give two reasons why a reaction time measured by the ruler-drop test may not be the same as a driver's reaction time on the road.
questions.model:
• The catcher may anticipate the drop, giving an unrealistically short time.
  • A driver must move a foot to the brake pedal, which takes longer than closing a hand.
  • The test is done while alert and expecting a signal; a real driver may be tired, distracted or not expecting a hazard.
  • (Any two.)

sections.title: Estimation in motion questions
sections.blurb: "Estimate the force on…" means: choose sensible values, say what you chose, calculate, and round. The method earns most of the marks.
checklist: Estimate the size of an everyday acceleration
Estimate the force in a typical road situation, stating the values you assume
Give an estimate to one or two significant figures with a unit

parts.title: How to answer an estimation question
parts.html:
An estimation question is marked on your method and sensible values, not on hitting one exact number. The examiner wants to see:

  1. Assumed values, written down with units — a mass, a speed, a time or distance. Use the typical values from the non-negotiables.
  2. The equations you are using.
  3. The calculation, to 1 or 2 significant figures.
  4. A sense check: compare the force with a weight, or the acceleration with $g$.
Useful assumed values
Mass of an adult70 kg
Mass of a car1000–1500 kg
Town speed (30 mph)13 m/s
Motorway speed (70 mph)30 m/s
Time for a car to pull away to 30 mphabout 5 s
Time to stop in a crashabout 0.1 s (0.5 s with a crumple zone)
Driver's reaction time0.7 s

Any answer within a factor of two or so of the examiner's will be accepted if your assumptions are stated and sensible. An unexplained number on its own is not.

parts.title: Estimating a crash force
parts.question: Estimate the force on a driver when a car travelling in town crashes into a wall.
steps: Assume: driver's mass $\approx 70$ kg; town speed $\approx 13$ m/s (30 mph); the driver stops in about $0.1$ s.
Sense check: about 13 times the driver's weight (700 N) — easily enough to cause serious injury, which is why cars have crumple zones and airbags.

parts.title: Estimation
parts.intro: Answers within about 20% of the model values are accepted — the method matters more than the exact number.

questions.text: Estimate the acceleration of a car pulling away from traffic lights and reaching the 30 mph limit.
questions.hint: 30 mph is about 13 m/s; a car takes roughly 5 s to get there.
walkthrough: Assume $v = 13$ m/s reached in $t = 5$ s from rest.
$a = \dfrac{13}{5} \approx 2.6$ m/s² — a few m/s², well under $g$.

questions.text: Estimate the force on a 60 kg bus passenger when the bus brakes sharply from 10 m/s to rest in 0.5 s.
questions.hint: Deceleration first, then F = ma.
walkthrough: $F = 60 \times 20 = 1200$ N — about twice her weight, which is why standing passengers get thrown forwards.

questions.text: Which is the best estimate of the force on a 1000 kg car during a motorway crash lasting 0.1 s?
questions.explain: a ≈ 30 ÷ 0.1 = 300 m/s², so F ≈ 1000 × 300 = 300 000 N. Thirty times the weight of the car.

questions.text: Describe how you would estimate the force on a cyclist who rides into a wall.
questions.model:
• Assume sensible values: the cyclist's mass (about 70 kg) and a typical cycling speed (about 6 m/s).
  • Assume a stopping time (around 0.1 s) or a stopping distance.
  • Calculate the deceleration from a = (v − u) ÷ t (or v² = 2ax), then the force from F = ma.
  • State the answer to 1 or 2 significant figures and compare it with the cyclist's weight.

questions.text: A sprinter crosses the finish line at 10 m/s and comes to a stop in about 2 s. Estimate her deceleration.
questions.hint: Change in speed ÷ time.

questions.text: Estimate the thinking distance of a car travelling at 30 mph in town.
questions.hint: 30 mph ≈ 13 m/s; a typical reaction time is about 0.7 s.
walkthrough: Thinking distance $= 13 \times 0.7 \approx 9$ m — matching the Highway Code's 9 m.

facts.a: Total momentum before = total momentum after, if no external forces
N3: equal and opposite forces → same time → equal and opposite Δp → total Δp = 0

facts.q: What provides the centripetal force for a car on a roundabout?
facts.a: Friction between the tyres and the road

facts.a: Gravity

facts.a: Both ×4 (∝ v²)

facts.q: An object falls at constant velocity. What is its acceleration?
facts.a: Zero. Constant velocity means no change in velocity, so the resultant force is zero and the acceleration is zero.

facts.a: g = 10 m/s² downwards, whatever its mass. Use it as a in the equations of motion.

facts.a: The resultant force — all the forces on the object added with their directions. Not the weight, unless the object is falling freely.

types.name: Speed, distance and time
types.method: Average speed is the distance travelled divided by the time taken. You need to recall this one: it is not on the equation sheet. Make sure the distance is in metres and the time in seconds before dividing, and to find distance or time, rearrange: distance = speed × time, time = distance / speed.
commonErrors: Dividing time by distance
Leaving the distance in km or the time in minutes
Averaging two speeds instead of dividing the total distance by the total time
Forgetting the unit, or writing m/s when the question asks for km/h

worked.question: A cyclist travels 120 m along a straight road in 8 s. Calculate the average speed of the cyclist.
steps: Known: distance = 120 m, time = 8 s. Unknown: average speed.

practice.question: A sprinter runs 200 m in 25 s. Calculate the average speed of the sprinter.
practice.hint: average speed = distance / time; both values are already in m and s.

practice.question: Thunder is heard 2.5 s after a lightning flash. Sound travels at 340 m/s. Calculate how far away the lightning was.
practice.hint: Rearrange to distance = speed × time.
walkthrough: speed = 340 m/s, time = 2.5 s, find distance.

practice.question: A car travels 36 km in 30 minutes. Calculate the average speed of the car in m/s.
practice.hint: Change 36 km to metres and 30 minutes to seconds before dividing.

practice.question: A walker moves at a steady 1.5 m/s. Calculate the time taken to walk 2.7 km. Give your answer in seconds.
practice.hint: Change 2.7 km to metres, then use time = distance / speed.
walkthrough: distance = 2.7 × 1000 = 2700 m, speed = 1.5 m/s, find time.

practice.question: A train travels 45 km in 25 minutes, then a further 15 km in 5 minutes. Calculate the average speed of the train for the whole journey in m/s.
practice.hint: Add up the total distance in metres and the total time in seconds, then divide.

practice.question: A runner covers the first 100 m of a race at 5 m/s and the second 100 m at 4 m/s. Calculate the average speed over the whole 200 m.
practice.hint: Find the time for each 100 m first (time = distance / speed), then divide the total distance by the total time.

types.name: Acceleration from a change in velocity
types.method: Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time taken: a = (v − u) / t, where u is the initial velocity and v the final velocity. Work out v − u first, then divide by t. If the object slows down, v − u is negative and so is the acceleration; a question asking for the deceleration wants the size of that value, without the minus sign.
commonErrors: Dividing the final velocity by the time instead of the change in velocity
Taking u − v instead of v − u and losing the sign
Forgetting to convert km/h to m/s before subtracting
Rearranging for v as v = a × t and forgetting to add u

worked.question: A motorbike speeds up from 5 m/s to 23 m/s in 4 s. Calculate its acceleration.
steps: Known: u = 5 m/s, v = 23 m/s, t = 4 s. Unknown: a.

practice.question: A sprinter leaves the blocks from rest and reaches 9 m/s after 3 s. Calculate the acceleration of the sprinter.
practice.hint: From rest means u = 0; use a = (v − u) / t.

practice.question: A train slows from 30 m/s to 12 m/s in 20 s as it approaches a station. Taking the direction of travel as positive, calculate the acceleration of the train.
practice.hint: v − u is negative because the train is slowing down; keep the minus sign in your answer.

practice.question: A cyclist travelling at 3 m/s accelerates at 0.5 m/s² for 8 s. Calculate the final velocity of the cyclist.
practice.hint: Rearrange to v = u + a × t.
walkthrough: u = 3 m/s, a = 0.5 m/s², t = 8 s, find v.
a = (v − u) / t → v = u + a × t

practice.question: A car accelerates from 54 km/h to 90 km/h in 5 s. Calculate the acceleration of the car in m/s².
practice.hint: Convert both speeds to m/s (× 1000, ÷ 3600) before finding the change in velocity.

practice.question: A lift starts from rest and accelerates upwards at 1.2 m/s² for 5 s. It then slows down steadily and stops 4 s later. Calculate the deceleration of the lift while it is slowing down.
practice.hint: Find the top speed first with v = u + a × t, then use that as u for the slowing-down part.
walkthrough: Slowing down: u = 6 m/s, v = 0, t = 4 s

practice.question: A car is travelling at 72 km/h when the driver brakes. The car decelerates at 4 m/s² until it stops. Calculate the time taken to stop.
practice.hint: Convert 72 km/h to m/s, take a = −4 m/s² and v = 0, then rearrange for t.
walkthrough: a = (v − u) / t → t = (v − u) / a

types.name: Velocity, acceleration and distance without time
types.method: Use this equation when a question gives a distance x but no time. Square the velocities first, then substitute. For an object dropped from rest u = 0; for an object thrown upwards v = 0 at the top and a = −10 m/s². When the unknown is v or u, you end up with v² or u², so take the square root as the last step.
commonErrors: Forgetting to square the velocities before substituting
Forgetting to take the square root at the end
Using a = +10 m/s² for an object moving upwards
Using this equation when a time is given and a = (v − u) / t is quicker

worked.question: A go-kart travelling at 5 m/s accelerates at 4 m/s² over a distance of 18 m. Calculate its final velocity.
steps: Known: u = 5 m/s, a = 4 m/s², x = 18 m. Unknown: v.
v² − u² = 2 × a × x → v² = u² + 2 × a × x

practice.question: A diver steps off a 5 m board and falls into the pool. Calculate the velocity of the diver when she reaches the water. Ignore air resistance.
practice.hint: u = 0 and a = g = 10 m/s²; find v² first, then take the square root.
walkthrough: u = 0, a = 10 m/s², x = 5 m, find v.

practice.question: A car accelerates from rest to 30 m/s over a distance of 150 m. Calculate the acceleration of the car.
practice.hint: Rearrange to a = (v² − u²) / (2 × x) with u = 0.
walkthrough: u = 0, v = 30 m/s, x = 150 m, find a.

practice.question: An aeroplane lands at 60 m/s and decelerates at 3 m/s² until it stops. Calculate the distance it travels along the runway.
practice.hint: v = 0 and a = −3 m/s²; rearrange to x = (v² − u²) / (2 × a).
walkthrough: u = 60 m/s, v = 0, a = −3 m/s², find x.

practice.question: A tennis ball is hit straight upwards and rises 11.25 m before it stops. Calculate the velocity at which it left the racket.
practice.hint: At the top v = 0 and a = −10 m/s²; rearrange for u² and take the square root.
walkthrough: v = 0, a = −10 m/s², x = 11.25 m, find u.
v² − u² = 2 × a × x → u² = v² − 2 × a × x

practice.question: A car travelling at 72 km/h brakes with a deceleration of 5 m/s². Calculate the distance the car travels before it stops.
practice.hint: Convert 72 km/h to m/s first; then v = 0 and a = −5 m/s², and rearrange for x.

practice.question: A toy rocket is launched straight up from a spring launcher and rises 320 cm before it stops. Calculate the velocity at which it left the launcher.
practice.hint: Change 320 cm to metres; at the top v = 0 and a = −10 m/s², so u² = −2 × a × x.

types.name: Reading a distance–time graph
equations: speed = gradient of a distance–time graph
average speed = total distance / total time
types.method: On a distance–time graph the gradient of a section is the speed: pick two points on the straight section where it crosses gridlines and divide the change in distance by the change in time. A flat section means the object is stationary; a steeper section means a higher speed. For an average speed over a whole journey, divide the total distance travelled by the total time, including any stops.
commonErrors: Reading the distance value instead of working out the gradient
Dividing the time by the distance
Using the time axis in minutes with distance in metres and calling the answer m/s
Leaving out the return journey when adding up the total distance travelled

worked.question: The graph shows the distance travelled by a runner. Use the graph to calculate the speed of the runner during the first 6 s.
steps: Speed is the gradient of the distance–time graph.
Pick two points on the first section: (0 s, 0 m) and A at (6 s, 30 m).
gradient = change in distance / change in time = (30 − 0) / (6 − 0)

practice.question: The graph shows the distance travelled by a cyclist. Use the graph to find how far the cyclist had travelled after 40 s, at the point marked P.
practice.hint: Go up from 40 s on the time axis to the line, then across to the distance axis.
walkthrough: Find 40 s on the time axis and go up to point P on the line.
Read across to the distance axis.
